1000022.etyen:
Borrowed from American English Egypt, for various place names in the United States. The individual American place names arose independently.
The name of Egypt in Arkansas is traditionally explained as an allusion to the abundance of corn grown in the area, compared with the corn of biblical Egypt. Egypt in Georgia was named after Egypt in reference to the country's fertile soil. Egypt in Pennsylvania, originally called Egypta, was likewise named in reference to the fertile land of ancient Egypt, regarded as the “granary of the world”. Egypt in Wharton County, Texas, was originally called Merce

1005142.etyen:
Compound of halleluja (“hallelujah”) + møte (“meeting”), literally “hallelujah meeting”.
The first element ultimately derives from Biblical Hebrew הַלְּלוּיָהּ (“praise Yah”), containing the masculine plural imperative of Biblical Hebrew הִלֵּל (“to praise”) and יָהּ (“Yah”), a shortened form of the divine name Biblical Hebrew יהוה (“Yahweh”).
The second element is an umlauted formation in the family of Old Norse mót (“meeting, encounter”) and mœta (“to meet”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *mōtą (“meeting”). Its further Indo-European derivation is uncertain.
